titre: The Silbo Gomero: Whistled Spanish That the Brain Reads as a Language
accroche: On La Gomera, people whistle Spanish. In 2005, MRI shows that the brains of those who understand it process it as speech.
contenu_vulgarise:
On La Gomera, a Canary island of deep ravines, a shepherd can address another from one slope to the other without raising his voice: he whistles. The silbo gomero is readily filed among folkloric curiosities, or among signal codes, halfway between birdsong and Morse. It is something else.

## Spanish, Without the Voice

According to the UNESCO notice, which inscribed it in 2009 on the list of intangible cultural heritage, the silbo reproduces through whistling the Castilian spoken by the islanders: each spoken vowel or consonant is replaced by a whistled sound. Two whistles stand in for the five Spanish vowels, four others for the consonants. They are distinguished by pitch and by whether the sound is continuous or interrupted. The count varies from study to study: the Wikipedia entry mentions from two to five vowels and from four to ten consonants.

The reduction has a cost. Several Spanish sounds fall on the same whistle, so a whistled sentence is more ambiguous than a spoken one. David Corina, one of the authors of the 2005 study, says so in the University of Washington press release: anything that can be said in Spanish can be translated into silbo, but context matters a great deal. The messages are, moreover, those of work: the press release cites opening a gate and the presence of a stray sheep. And it is not a mother tongue: according to the same press release, children are not born whistling it.

## What the Brain Does with It

In 2005, Manuel Carreiras (University of La Laguna, Tenerife), David Corina (University of Washington), Jorge Lopez and Francisco Rivero publish a functional MRI study in *Nature*. It compares five silbadores (whistlers), who also speak Spanish, with five Spanish speakers who do not understand silbo.

Faced with sentences in Spanish, both groups show the same pattern of activity, in both hemispheres. Faced with sentences in silbo, the silbadores activate, on the left, the posterior temporo-parietal region and the frontal premotor cortex, plus the right temporal lobe. The others activate several regions, but none that is specifically associated with language processing. Same whistles, two brains, two kinds of processing. The sample is small, ten people, which invites reading the result as a clue rather than as definitive proof.

## What This Shifts

What makes a signal a language is therefore not the channel. The same system of left-hemisphere regions that processes speech also processes, in those who know it, a whistle: Corina reads in this a specialization of those regions for communication, independent of the modality of the signal. What the brain recognizes is an organization it has learned, not a timbre. Silbo, incidentally, has no grammar of its own: it has only that of Spanish, transposed.

What remains is the fate of this transposition. The telephone reduced its practical use, and since 1999 silbo has been taught in school on the island. What becomes of a whistled language when no one needs to make themselves heard from one slope to the other?

repere.texte: While listening to sentences in silbo, the five silbadores tested activate left-hemisphere language regions; the five Spanish speakers who do not understand it activate several regions, none of which is specifically associated with language processing.
repere.source: Carreiras, Lopez, Rivero & Corina, “Linguistic perception: Neural processing of a whistled language,” Nature 433, 31-32, 2005; results reported in the University of Washington press release of January 6, 2005

carte.punch: On La Gomera, people whistle Spanish. Only those who understand it listen to it as a language.
carte.idee: The silbo gomero replaces the vowels and consonants of Spanish with whistles. In 2005, an MRI study of ten people shows that only the silbadores process these whistles with language regions: what makes a language is the system you know, not the channel.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The 2009 inscription notice and the safeguarding measures.

quiz.question: What does the 2005 MRI show in Spanish speakers who do not understand silbo when they listen to it?
choix: Activated regions, but none specifically associated with language
Stronger activity than in the silbadores, as the brain tries to decode the message
No brain activity at all, since whistling is not a speech sound
The same activity as in the silbadores, because the brain processes every articulated sound as speech
quiz.explication: Non-speakers activate several regions, but none specifically linked to language, whereas the silbadores activate language regions on the left. Whistling is not silent to the brain, but it is not processed there as language: what makes these sounds a language is knowledge of the system they transpose.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does the silbo gomero transpose Castilian, according to the UNESCO notice?
choix: Each Spanish word receives a single whistle, unrelated to its sounds
Two whistles stand in for the vowels, four for the consonants
Only the vowels are whistled, the consonants being spoken in a low voice
Silbo follows a grammar of its own, different from that of Spanish
quiz_supplementaire.explication: UNESCO describes two whistles for the vowels and four for the consonants, distinguished by pitch and by whether the whistled sound is continuous or interrupted.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which regions do the five silbadores tested in 2005 activate when listening to sentences in silbo?
choix: Only the visual cortex, since silbo would be processed as a sound image
The same regions as for music, with no region associated with language
No specific region, with activity remaining diffuse throughout the brain
The left posterior temporo-parietal region, the frontal premotor cortex, and the right temporal lobe
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The silbadores activate, on the left, the posterior temporo-parietal region and the frontal premotor cortex, as well as the right temporal lobe, when listening to silbo.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does David Corina say, in the University of Washington press release, about translating Spanish into silbo?
choix: Only short everyday sentences can be translated into silbo
Only proper names and numbers translate faithfully into silbo
Anything that can be said in Spanish can be translated into silbo, but context matters a great deal
Nothing can really be translated: silbo remains a signal code, not a language
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Corina states that any Spanish utterance can be translated into silbo, but stresses that context matters a great deal, since the reduction in sounds makes sentences more ambiguous.
